method: A closed GOP starts on a keyframe and repeats at the encoder's keyframe interval, so at a constant frame rate the keyframes fall on whole multiples of the GOP length counted from frame zero of the file. The page turns the interval in seconds into a whole-frame GOP length as the interval multiplied by the frame rate, rounded, and never shorter than one frame. Both timecodes then become frame numbers: hours times 3600 plus minutes times 60 plus seconds, all times the nominal frame count round(fps) (24 for 23.976, 30 for 29.97, 60 for 59.94), plus the frame number, less two frame numbers for every minute that is not a multiple of ten when the timecode is drop-frame at 29.97 (four at 59.94). A semicolon marks drop-frame and a colon non-drop, the two notations cannot be mixed in one plan, and a drop-frame label that names a skipped frame is refused. The aligned range runs from floor(in / GOP) * GOP to ceil((out + 1) / GOP) * GOP, exclusive at the end, so it starts and ends on keyframes and contains the requested cut. Preroll is the distance from the aligned start to the in point, the tail is the distance from the last kept frame to the aligned end, and their sum is the footage outside the cut that a frame-accurate trim has to decode. The out point is inclusive, so 00:00:10:10 to 00:00:11:24 at 25 fps keeps forty frames. The model assumes a closed GOP with a keyframe exactly every interval and no keyframes from scene cuts; open GOPs, variable intervals and encoder-side scene detection move the real boundaries, so the table of five keyframes is a plan to check against the file's own keyframe list before a lossless export. Inputs allow 1 to 240 fps, intervals from 0.1 to 60 seconds and timecodes up to 23:59:59. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched.

sources.title: SMPTE timecode - Wikipedia: drop-frame timecode skips two frame numbers each minute except every tenth minute at 29.97 fps, which keeps the labels aligned with real time
